shortTheory.question: What are temporary and permanent magnets?
shortTheory.answer: Temporary magnets are the magnets that work in the presence of a magnetic field of permanent magnets. Once the magnetic field vanishes, they lose their magnetic properties. Permanent magnets retain their magnetic properties forever.

shortTheory.question: Define magnetic field of a magnet.
shortTheory.answer: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where an other magnetic object experiences a force on it.

shortTheory.question: What are magnetic lines of force?
shortTheory.answer: This pattern can be better shown by lines that correspond to the path of the filings. These lines are called magnetic lines of force.

shortTheory.question: Name some uses of permanent magnets and electromagnets.
shortTheory.answer: Permanent magnets are used in electric motors, electric generators, moving coil loudspeakers, separating iron objects from different mixtures etc. Electromagnets are temporary magnets. They are used in electric bells, magnetic relays, circuit breakers, telephone receivers, electromagnetic cranes, etc.

definitions.text: Magnetism is a force that acts at a distance upon magnetic materials.
Magnetic material such as iron or steel can be made a magnet. This is known as magnetization. In other words, we can say that magnetism has induced in it.
Temporary magnets are the magnets that work in the presence of a magnetic field of permanent magnets. Once the magnetic field vanishes, they lose their magnetic properties.
Permanent magnets retain their magnetic properties forever.
A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where an other magnetic object experiences a force on it.
This pattern can be better shown by lines that correspond to the path of the filings. These lines are called magnetic lines of force.
The direction of the magnetic field at any point in space is the direction indicated by the N-pole of a magnetic compass needle placed at that point.
The strength of the magnetic field is proportional to the number of magnetic lines of force passing through unit area placed perpendicular to the lines.
An iron nail or a rod becomes a magnet when an electric current passes through a coil of wire around it. It is called an electromagnet.

Grip the solenoid with the right hand such that fingers are curled along the direction of current (positive to the negative terminal of the battery) in the solenoid, then the thumb points to the N-pole of the bar end.

formulas.formula: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
formulas.use: Use this law to predict whether two magnetic poles will attract or repel. No quantities or SI units apply.

formulas.formula: Magnetic field strength ∝ number of magnetic lines of force passing through unit area perpendicular to the lines.
formulas.use: Use the spacing or density of field lines to compare field strength. No numerical quantities or SI units are specified in this chapter.

formulas.formula: More turns in the coil or greater current → stronger electromagnet.
formulas.use: Use to explain how to increase an electromagnet’s strength. Current is measured in amperes (A); the number of turns is a count and has no SI unit.

formulas.formula: Outside a magnet, field lines appear to go from N to S.
formulas.use: Use to show the direction of field lines around a bar magnet. No quantities or SI units apply.

fullMarks: For a definition question, write the complete textbook definition rather than only a keyword or example.
For a question about identifying a magnet, describe the test with a suspended bar magnet: attraction alone is not conclusive; repulsion by one pole confirms the object is a magnet.
For field-line diagrams, draw clear curved lines with arrows, show the N and S poles, and keep the lines closer together where the field is stronger.

For the solenoid magnetisation diagram, draw the steel bar inside the coil, show the battery and current direction, label ends A and B, and apply the right-hand grip rule to make A the N-pole and B the S-pole.
When asked for uses, give named examples and distinguish permanent magnets from electromagnets; state that an electromagnet works while current passes through its coil.
For a long explanation, write the key principle first, then explain the steps in order, and finish by stating the result.
If a question asks for a diagram, draw it large enough to read and label every part specifically requested.

mistakes: Mistake: Saying attraction proves an object is a magnet. Fix: Attraction can also be caused by induced magnetism in a magnetic material; repulsion by a pole is the definite test.
Mistake: Reversing the pole rule. Fix: Remember and write, “Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.”
Mistake: Drawing field lines without arrows or with lines crossing. Fix: Add arrows to show direction and draw field lines without crossings.
Mistake: Saying a temporary magnet keeps its magnetism after the external field or current is removed. Fix: State that it loses its magnetic properties when the field vanishes or the current stops.
Mistake: Applying the right-hand grip rule with the fingers following the wrong direction. Fix: Curl the fingers in the direction of current through the solenoid; the thumb points to its N-pole.
Mistake: Claiming a single isolated N-pole or S-pole can be made by breaking a magnet. Fix: State that every piece has both a north and a south pole.
